newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thomson BankWatch downgrades Thai bank ratings.
newsitem.headline: Thomson BankWatch downgrades Thai bank ratings.

text.p: Thomson BankWatch-Asia said on Wednesday it downgraded ratings of six major Thai commercial banks with immediate effect to reflect sharp deterioration of their asset quality.

Thamson Bankwatch said in a statement that it downgraded intra-country issuer ratings of Bangkok Bank Plc, Thai Farmers Bank Plc, Siam Commercial Bank Plc, Krung Thai Bank Plc, Bank of Ayudhya Plc, and Thai Military Bank Plc.
It said short-term local currency debt ratings of these banks except Krung Thai were also downgraded.
Thomson BankWatch, however, retained Thailand's sovereign risk rating at A-.
It said of the bank downgrades: "These downgrades primarily reflect sharp deterioration in asset quality, stemming primarily from a slowing Thai economy and troubled real estate market."

"As conditions in Thailand are expected to remain difficult in 1997, further deterioration in asset quality is expected to occur. Krung Thai Bank's ratings are underpinned by its position as the only government controlled institution."

It said the intra-country issuer ratings of Bangkok Bank, Thai Farmers and Siam Commercial were downgraded to IC-C from IC-B, that of Krung Thai to IC-B/C from IC-B, and those of Bank of Ayudhya and Thai Military to IC-C/D from IC-C.

Short-term local currency debt ratings of Bangkok Bank, Thai Farmers, Siam Commercial and Thai Military were also downgraded to LC-2 from LC-1, and that of Bank of Ayudhya to LC-3 from LC-2. The related rating for Krung Thai was retained at its current LC-1.

Philippe Delhaise, president of Thomson BankWatch-Asia, said Thailand's unfavourable interest rate environment and a glut of properties will continue to compromise the ability of real estate-related companies to service debts.

He said Thai banks have sizeable exposure to real estate, not only in the form of loans to real estate developers but to construction companies, hotels, various other business tied to the real estate industry and residential mortgages.

Betty Starkey, Thomson BankWatch's director of sovereign risk, said: "Thailand currently faces a challenging dilemma that defies any simple solution. A gaping current account deficit is forcing monetary authorities to keep interest rates at lofty levels to protect the local currency and prevent foreign capital from leaving the country."

She said the government of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh faced an enormous challenge of restoring public confidence in its ability to manage the current crisis, stabilise the economy and steer the financial sector clear of collapse.
"BankWatch is closely monitoring these developments, we believe that our current A- rating on Thailand remains appropriate and reflects the level of volatility and risk inherent in the Thai market."
